```{r, include = FALSE}
has_sf <- requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  eval = has_sf
)
```

```{r setup}
library(a5R)
```

A *covering* is a set of A5 cells at one resolution that stands for an area:
the cells of a polygon, of a disk around a cell, or of a cap of a given
radius. a5R stores each covering compacted. Every complete group of sibling
cells is replaced by its parent, and a trailing *compaction marker* records
the resolution the stored cells stand for. An `a5_covering` vector holds one
covering per element, so coverings sit in a data frame column next to the
features they describe.

Combining, testing and measuring coverings works on the compacted cells
directly, without expanding them, so it stays fast for coverings that stand
for millions of cells.

## Building coverings

`a5_polygon_to_cells()` returns one covering per feature. Here, every county
of North Carolina at resolution 11, where a cell covers about 8 km²:

```{r polygons, message = FALSE}
library(sf)
nc <- st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"), quiet = TRUE)
nc <- st_transform(nc, 4326) # A5 works in WGS 84 longitude and latitude
nc$cells <- a5_polygon_to_cells(nc, resolution = 11)
nc[1:4, c("NAME", "cells")]
```

Each covering prints its resolution, the number of cells it stands for, and
the number it stores. `a5_spherical_cap()`, `a5_grid_disk()` and
`a5_cell_to_subcell()` return one covering per centre cell, and
`a5_compact()` turns any set of cells into one:

```{r others}
raleigh <- a5_lonlat_to_cell(-78.64, 35.78, resolution = 11)
near_raleigh <- a5_spherical_cap(raleigh, radius = 60000)
near_raleigh

a5_grid_disk(raleigh, k = 5)
a5_compact(a5_cell_to_children(raleigh, resolution = 13))
```

## Measuring coverings

`a5_count()` gives the number of cells a covering stands for and `a5_area()`
its area. A5 cells are equal-area, so the area is the count times the area
of one cell. At resolution 11 it tracks each county's area closely:

```{r measures}
nc$cell_area <- a5_area(nc$cells, units = "km^2")
nc$true_area <- units::set_units(st_area(nc), "km^2")
head(nc[c("NAME", "cell_area", "true_area")], 4)

err <- as.numeric((nc$cell_area - nc$true_area) / nc$true_area)
round(100 * stats::quantile(abs(err), c(0.5, 0.9, 1)), 1)
```

The error is under 1% for the median county and about 6% at worst. A
covering counts whole cells, and each cell straddling a county boundary is
in or out by its centre. Finer resolutions reduce the error.

## Combining coverings

`a5_union()`, `a5_intersect()` and `a5_difference()` combine coverings
element by element, recycling a length-one argument. With a single argument,
`a5_union()` merges every covering in a vector into one:

```{r combine}
state <- a5_union(nc$cells)
state

a5_intersect(state, near_raleigh)
counties_near <- a5_intersect(nc$cells, near_raleigh)
nc$NAME[a5_count(counties_near) > 0]
```

```{r combine-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.2, echo = -c(1, 9)}
op <- par(mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(st_geometry(nc), border = "#bbbbbb", lwd = 0.5)
plot(a5_cell_to_boundary(a5_uncompact(a5_difference(state, near_raleigh))),
     col = "#206ead30", border = NA, add = TRUE)
plot(a5_cell_to_boundary(a5_uncompact(a5_intersect(state, near_raleigh))),
     col = "#d9534f80", border = NA, add = TRUE)
plot(a5_cell_to_lonlat(raleigh), pch = 19, cex = 0.6, add = TRUE)
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", fill = c("#d9534f80", "#206ead30"),
       border = NA, legend = c("Within 60 km of Raleigh", "Rest of the state"))
par(op)
```

Both coverings in each pair must be at the same resolution. A5 cells do not
nest geometrically across resolutions, so combining sets at different
resolutions has no meaning, and it is an error:

```{r mismatch, error = TRUE}
a5_union(state, a5_spherical_cap(a5_cell_to_parent(raleigh), radius = 60000))
```

## Testing coverings

`a5_contains()` tests cells against a covering. Indexing points at the
covering's resolution turns it into a point-in-polygon test:

```{r contains}
set.seed(1)
lon <- stats::runif(1000, -84.5, -75.5)
lat <- stats::runif(1000, 33.8, 36.6)
points <- a5_lonlat_to_cell(lon, lat, resolution = a5_covering_resolution(state))
in_state <- a5_contains(state, points)
mean(in_state)
```

The answer agrees with an exact geometric test except for a few points in
cells that straddle the state boundary, all within one cell of it:

```{r contains-check}
exact <- lengths(st_intersects(
  st_as_sf(data.frame(lon, lat), coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = st_crs(nc)),
  st_union(nc)
)) > 0
table(covering = in_state, exact = exact)
```

`a5_overlaps()` tests whether two coverings share any cell. With the default
centre containment, every cell belongs to the one county holding its centre,
so the county coverings partition the state and no two overlap. With
`containment = "overlapping"`, cells along a shared border belong to both
counties:

```{r overlaps}
ashe <- nc$cells[nc$NAME == "Ashe"]
neighbours <- nc$NAME %in% c("Alleghany", "Wilkes", "Watauga")
a5_overlaps(nc$cells[neighbours], ashe)

gap_free <- a5_polygon_to_cells(nc[nc$NAME %in% c("Ashe", "Alleghany", "Wilkes", "Watauga"), ],
                                resolution = 11, containment = "overlapping")
a5_overlaps(gap_free[-1], gap_free[1])
```

## Drawing and joining

The stored cells of a covering have mixed resolutions and are parents in
the A5 index, whose outlines do not nest geometrically: drawn directly, they
would show overlaps and gaps. `a5_uncompact()` expands coverings to their
cells, which is what to plot or join to data keyed by cell:

```{r uncompact}
cells <- a5_uncompact(nc$cells[1:3])
length(cells)
all(a5_get_resolution(cells) == 11)

per_county <- a5_uncompact(nc$cells[1:3], simplify = FALSE)
lengths(per_county)
```

`simplify = FALSE` keeps one element per covering, ready for
`tidyr::unnest()`. Uncompacting can build a great many cells: a covering of
France at resolution 18 stands for about a billion. `a5_uncompact()` refuses
to build more than `.Machine$integer.max` cells; work with the covering
itself where possible.

## Storing coverings

Coverings keep their compaction marker in storage, as in the other A5
libraries. `a5_covering_to_arrow()` writes them to an Arrow `list<uint64>`
column that DuckDB, Python and JavaScript read with the resolution intact,
and `a5_covering_from_arrow()` reads them back, normalising coverings
written elsewhere. See `vignette("arrow-parquet")`. For coverings built by
hand from outside data, `as_a5_covering()` sorts and compacts them, and
`a5_is_valid()` checks that a covering is well formed.
